q: Organic chemistry is defined as the branch of chemistry that deals with:
o: All compounds that contain carbon, including carbonates
x: Organic chemistry is the study of compounds of carbon with hydrogen (hydrocarbons) and the compounds derived from them. Carbonates, CO and CO₂ contain carbon but are studied as inorganic compounds.

q: In almost all organic compounds, each carbon atom forms how many covalent bonds?
x: Carbon has four valence electrons (2s² 2p²) and is tetravalent, forming four covalent bonds in organic compounds, as in CH₄.

q: The vital force theory was rejected after Wöhler (1828) prepared urea in the laboratory by heating:
x: Wöhler heated ammonium cyanate (NH₄CNO), an inorganic salt, and obtained urea, an organic compound from living things. This showed organic compounds could be made without a living organism.

q: According to the vital force theory, organic compounds:
o: Could be made only from minerals
Could be made only inside living organisms
Could be made in the laboratory from any element
x: The vital force theory held that a 'vital force' present only in living things was needed to make organic compounds, so they could not be prepared in the laboratory. Wöhler's synthesis of urea disproved it.

q: The ability of carbon atoms to link with one another to form long chains and rings is called:
x: Catenation is self-linking of carbon atoms into chains and rings. It is the main reason for the enormous number of organic compounds; isomerism adds further variety.

q: Which property is generally typical of organic compounds?
o: They are mostly covalent and have relatively low melting points
They are mostly ionic and have very high melting points
They usually dissolve in water and conduct electricity
They do not burn when heated in air
x: Most organic compounds are covalent, so they have low melting and boiling points, are usually non-electrolytes, are more soluble in organic solvents than in water, and are generally combustible.

q: Which of the following carbon compounds is classed as an organic compound?
x: Ethanoic acid (acetic acid), CH₃COOH, is a derivative of a hydrocarbon. CO₂, carbonates such as Na₂CO₃ and cyanides such as KCN contain carbon but are treated as inorganic compounds.

q: Which of the following is a major natural source of organic compounds?
x: Petroleum (with coal, natural gas, plants and animals) is a main source of organic compounds. Limestone contains carbon only as calcium carbonate, which is inorganic; bauxite and rock salt are inorganic minerals.

q: Reactions of organic compounds are generally slower than reactions between ionic compounds in solution because:
o: They involve breaking and forming covalent bonds
They involve free ions that repel each other
Organic compounds have very high lattice energies
x: Organic reactions need covalent bonds to be broken and new ones formed, which requires activation energy and takes time. Ionic reactions in solution involve ions that are already free and combine almost instantly.

q: Which statement is correct?
o: Every compound of carbon is an organic compound
Every organic compound contains carbon, but not every carbon compound is organic
Organic compounds can be obtained only from living things
x: All organic compounds contain carbon, but compounds such as CO, CO₂, carbonates and cyanides are inorganic. Many organic compounds (e.g. methane) contain no oxygen, and they can be made in the laboratory.

q: Organic compounds whose carbon atoms form straight or branched chains but no rings are called:
x: Open-chain, also called acyclic or aliphatic, compounds have carbon atoms joined in straight or branched chains, e.g. butane. Homocyclic, heterocyclic and aromatic compounds all contain rings.

q: Cyclohexane (C₆H₁₂) is classified as:
x: Cyclohexane has a ring made only of carbon atoms (homocyclic) with no benzene ring, and it behaves like an aliphatic compound, so it is alicyclic. Benzene, not cyclohexane, is aromatic.

q: Benzene and naphthalene belong to the class of:
x: Compounds containing one or more benzene rings, such as benzene and naphthalene, are aromatic (benzenoid). Their rings contain only carbon atoms, so they are homocyclic, not heterocyclic.

q: Pyridine (C₅H₅N) is classified as a heterocyclic compound because:
o: Its ring contains only carbon atoms
Its ring contains a nitrogen atom as well as carbon atoms
It has an open chain of carbon atoms
It contains a benzene ring joined to a side chain
x: A heterocyclic compound has at least one atom other than carbon (such as N, O or S) in its ring. In pyridine one ring atom is nitrogen.

q: Which of the following is a homocyclic (carbocyclic) compound?
x: Toluene's ring is made only of carbon atoms, so it is homocyclic (and aromatic). Furan has O, thiophene has S and pyrrole has N in the ring, so they are heterocyclic.

q: The heteroatom present in the ring of thiophene is:
x: Thiophene is a five-membered ring with four carbon atoms and one sulphur atom ('thio' means sulphur). Furan contains oxygen and pyrrole contains nitrogen.

q: Which pair contains two heterocyclic compounds?
x: Furan (O in ring) and pyrrole (N in ring) are both heterocyclic. Benzene, toluene and naphthalene are aromatic homocyclic compounds, and cyclohexane and cyclopropane are alicyclic.

q: Isobutane, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃, is an example of:
x: Isobutane (2-methylpropane) has no ring, so it is open-chain, and its middle carbon carries a CH₃ branch, so the chain is branched. Butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, is the straight-chain isomer.

q: Cyclopropane (C₃H₆) is correctly classified as:
x: Cyclopropane has a ring (closed-chain), the ring contains only carbon (homocyclic), and it has no benzene ring, so it is alicyclic. A heterocyclic ring would contain an atom other than carbon.

q: The term 'alicyclic' refers to compounds that are:
o: Cyclic and contain at least one benzene ring
Cyclic with an atom other than carbon in the ring
Cyclic but similar to aliphatic compounds in their properties
x: 'Alicyclic' combines aliphatic and cyclic: carbon rings, such as cyclohexane, whose properties resemble those of open-chain (aliphatic) compounds. Rings of the benzene type are aromatic.

q: A functional group is:
o: An atom or group of atoms that gives an organic compound its characteristic properties
The longest chain of carbon atoms in a molecule
A group of compounds differing from each other by CH₂
The ring of carbon atoms in a cyclic compound
x: A functional group, such as –OH or –COOH, is the reactive part of a molecule that largely decides its chemical properties. A series differing by CH₂ is a homologous series.

q: The functional group of carboxylic acids is:
x: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group, –COOH, as in ethanoic acid CH₃COOH. –CHO is aldehyde, –OH is alcohol and –COOR is ester.

q: Ethanal (acetaldehyde), CH₃CHO, contains which functional group?
x: The –CHO group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to at least one hydrogen, is the aldehyde group. In a ketone the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon atoms.

q: Propanone (acetone), CH₃COCH₃, belongs to which class of compounds?
x: In CH₃COCH₃ the carbonyl group (C=O) is bonded to two carbon atoms, which makes it a ketone. An aldehyde has the carbonyl at the end of the chain bonded to H.

q: Methoxymethane (dimethyl ether), CH₃OCH₃, contains which functional group?
x: In CH₃OCH₃ an oxygen atom joins two alkyl groups, the ether linkage R–O–R. It has no O–H bond, so it is not an alcohol, and no C=O, so it is neither ester nor ketone.

q: Ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate), CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, contains which functional group?
x: The –COO– group with an alkyl group on the oxygen (–COOR) is the ester group. A carboxylic acid would have –COOH, with H in place of the alkyl group.

q: Ethanamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂, contains which functional group?
x: The –NH₂ group attached to an alkyl carbon is the amino group of amines. An amide has –NH₂ attached to a carbonyl carbon (–CONH₂).

q: Ethanenitrile (methyl cyanide), CH₃CN, contains which functional group?
x: CH₃CN contains the –C≡N group, with the carbon of the group bonded to the methyl group, so it is a nitrile (cyanide). In an isocyanide the alkyl group is bonded to the nitrogen.

q: Which pair of compounds has the same molecular formula but different functional groups?
x: Propanal (aldehyde) and propanone (ketone) are both C₃H₆O. Ethanol and propanol differ by CH₂, ethanoic acid and methyl ethanoate have different formulas, and butane and isobutane have no different functional groups (they differ only in chain).

q: Which compound contains both a hydroxyl (–OH) group and a carboxyl (–COOH) group?
x: Lactic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH, has an alcoholic –OH on the second carbon and a –COOH group. CH₃COCH₂OH has a ketone and an –OH, CH₃COOCH₃ is an ester, and HOCH₂CH₂OH has two –OH groups.

q: Stereoisomers are compounds that have:
o: The same structural formula but different arrangements of atoms in space
The same molecular formula but different structural formulas
Different molecular formulas but the same functional group
The same molecular mass but different elements
x: In stereoisomers the atoms are joined in the same order (same structural formula) but are arranged differently in space. Same molecular formula with different structural formulas describes structural isomers.

q: Which compound shows geometric (cis–trans) isomerism?
x: In but-2-ene each doubly bonded carbon carries two different groups (H and CH₃), so cis and trans forms exist. In the others at least one double-bond carbon carries two identical groups (two H atoms or two CH₃ groups).

q: For an alkene to show geometric isomerism, it must have:
o: Free rotation about the C=C bond
A carbon atom attached to four different groups
Restricted rotation about the C=C bond and two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon
At least two identical groups on one doubly bonded carbon
x: The π bond prevents rotation about C=C, and each doubly bonded carbon must carry two different groups so that 'same side' and 'opposite side' arrangements differ. Four different groups on one carbon is the condition for optical isomerism.

q: Which compound does NOT show cis–trans isomerism?
x: In CH₂=CCl₂ one carbon has two H atoms and the other two Cl atoms, so swapping groups gives the same molecule. Each of the other three has two different groups on both doubly bonded carbons.

q: Which statement about cis- and trans-1,2-dichloroethene (ClCH=CHCl) is correct?
o: Both isomers have zero dipole moment
The cis isomer is polar, while in the trans isomer the C–Cl bond dipoles cancel
The trans isomer is polar, while the cis isomer has zero dipole moment
x: In the cis isomer both Cl atoms are on the same side, so the C–Cl bond dipoles add and the molecule is polar. In the trans isomer they point in opposite directions and cancel. Both are C₂H₂Cl₂.

q: A chiral (asymmetric) carbon atom is one that is:
o: Bonded to two identical and two different groups
Bonded to four different atoms or groups
Part of a carbon–carbon double bond
x: A carbon with four different groups attached has a mirror image that cannot be superimposed on it, so it is chiral and can give optical isomers. If any two groups are identical, the carbon is not chiral.

q: Which compound is optically active?
x: In butan-2-ol the second carbon bears H, OH, CH₃ and C₂H₅, four different groups, so it is chiral. In propan-2-ol that carbon has two CH₃ groups, and glycine and ethanol have no carbon with four different groups.

q: The two enantiomers of lactic acid differ from each other in:
o: The direction in which they rotate plane-polarised light
x: Enantiomers have identical physical properties such as melting and boiling points, but rotate plane-polarised light by the same angle in opposite directions (dextrorotatory and laevorotatory).

q: A racemic mixture is optically inactive because:
o: Its molecules have a plane of symmetry
Its molecules cannot interact with light
It contains equal amounts of two enantiomers whose rotations cancel
x: A racemic mixture is a 50 : 50 mixture of the (+) and (−) enantiomers. Each molecule is chiral, but the equal and opposite rotations cancel, so the mixture shows no net rotation.

q: Which compound shows both geometric and optical isomerism?
x: Pent-3-en-2-ol has two different groups on each carbon of C=C (geometric) and a carbon bearing H, OH, CH₃ and CH=CHCH₃ (chiral). But-2-ene is only geometric, butan-2-ol only optical, and the last compound shows neither.

q: How many chiral carbon atoms are present in 3-chlorobutan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH(Cl)CH₃?
x: Carbon-2 carries H, OH, CH₃ and CH(Cl)CH₃; carbon-3 carries H, Cl, CH₃ and CH(OH)CH₃. Both have four different groups, so there are 2 chiral carbons; the two CH₃ carbons are not chiral.
